items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: that night I met the pianist. His name was Ellis Larkins

ctx.x: I was surprised because Teddy Wilson had told me two years before that Barney Josephson had said that he never wanted Al and myself in his place again. I accepted to replace Billy until he came out of the hospital and that night I met the pianist. His name was Ellis Larkins, was from Baltimore and had been studying at Julliard music college on a scholarship he had won in his home town.

Teddy Wilson was still in the club with Joe Thomas on trumpet John Williams, bass, and Sid Catlett, drums. I don't remember who was playing sax, but Benny Morton was still with the band. The show had Hazel Scott, the Golden Gate Quartet, two sisters who danced East Indian dances named the Craft Sisters, Pete Johnson and Albert Ammons, the two boogie woogie pianists. With our trio of piano, bass and trumpet, we took care of the dancing. It was the first time that I played with only a piano and bass. Our salary was…

After two weeks, Barney was satisfied with the trio as it was, Teddy and his musicians enjoyed us, and we went well with the customers, so Billy Moore was out and I was in. We decided to split the leader's fee between us, and that made each of us have 80 dollars a week. When the last show went on at 2 a.m., we were finished for the night, so we were able to be at the White Rose Bar at 52nd street and Sixth Avenue, before the musicians on Swing Street finished.
